# Public Evidence Chain: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Software Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive assessment

The strongest public evidence indicates that the 2023 compromise of 3CX DesktopApp began with a **prior compromise of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software**, not with an initial intrusion directly against the 3CX application. A 3CX employee later installed the maliciously modified X_TRADER package, enabling the attackers to enter and move through the 3CX environment. The attackers subsequently compromised 3CX’s Windows and macOS build environments, inserted malicious code into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp installers, and distributed trojanized versions to 3CX customers.

This conclusion is based primarily on Mandiant’s incident-response findings, which identified the X_TRADER compromise as the initial intrusion vector and described the event as the first confirmed case in which one software supply-chain compromise led to another ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]). The downstream campaign affected potentially hundreds of thousands of organizations because 3CX reported approximately 600,000 corporate customers and more than 12 million daily active users, although the number of organizations that actually executed a malicious version and the number that received follow-on payloads were substantially smaller or uncertain ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/) [S1]; [WIRED, 2023a](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/) [S2]).

The activity was publicly associated with a **North Korea-linked threat nexus**, but naming varied among reporting organizations. CrowdStrike linked the activity to Labyrinth Chollima, while Mandiant tracked the operational cluster as **UNC4736** and assessed with moderate confidence that it was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky attributed the deployment of the Gopuram backdoor to Lazarus with medium to high confidence. MITRE ATT&CK records AppleJeus as malware used by Lazarus Group. Accordingly, the most defensible characterization is: **UNC4736, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster, publicly associated with Lazarus/AppleJeus-related activity; exact subgroup attribution remains uncertain** ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]; [Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4]; [MITRE, 2025](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/) [S6]).

## Scope and source hierarchy

This reconstruction uses the supplied public reporting and distinguishes between:

- **Observed facts**, such as identified malware, file paths, hashes, affected versions, and build-environment activity.
- **Vendor assessments**, such as Mandiant’s assessment concerning UNC4736 and North Korean AppleJeus activity.
- **Media descriptions or early reporting**, which may reflect preliminary attribution or incomplete visibility.
- **Unresolved issues**, including the precise operator identity, the full victim set, and whether cryptocurrency theft was completed.

Mandiant’s report receives the greatest evidentiary weight for reconstructing the intrusion chain because it describes direct incident-response findings inside the 3CX environment. Kaspersky’s telemetry is especially important for identifying the targeted deployment of Gopuram. Google TAG and MITRE provide relevant historical context concerning AppleJeus and Lazarus but do not, by themselves, prove that every 3CX action was performed by the same subgroup.

## Reconstructed intrusion and propagation chain

### Stage 1: Prior compromise of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER

Mandiant identified a trojanized installer named `X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe`, with MD5 hash `ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`. The software was associated with Trading Technologies and remained available from the legitimate Trading Technologies website even though the X_TRADER platform had reportedly been discontinued in 2020. The installer and its embedded `Setup.exe` were digitally signed with a certificate subject identifying “Trading Technologies International, Inc.” ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]).

The malicious X_TRADER installer deployed a multi-stage modular backdoor called **VEILEDSIGNAL**. Its execution relied on two trojanized DLLs and a benign executable. The benign executable was used to sideload a malicious DLL, after which SIGFLIP and DAVESHELL were used to decrypt and load the final payload into memory. Mandiant observed that this X_TRADER loading process was materially similar to the loading process later used in the 3CX compromise, including use of the same RC4 key, `3jB(2bsG#@c7`, and the same general SIGFLIP/DAVESHELL technique ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]).

Mandiant’s central finding was that a 3CX employee’s computer had been compromised after the employee downloaded or installed the malicious X_TRADER package. This provided the attackers with an initial foothold in the 3CX network. WIRED summarized the finding as a supply-chain “chain reaction”: the first compromised software product enabled the compromise of a second software producer, whose application was then distributed to its customers ([WIRED, 2023b](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two) [S8]).

The exact mechanism by which the X_TRADER package was initially altered remains unresolved in the supplied evidence. Mandiant did not investigate the original Trading Technologies compromise, and therefore could not determine how the X_TRADER application was modified or how many other victims may have received it ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]; [WIRED, 2023b](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two) [S8]).

### Stage 2: Intrusion into and lateral movement within 3CX

Once the attacker obtained access through the compromised X_TRADER installation, Mandiant reconstructed lateral movement inside the 3CX environment. The attackers harvested credentials and moved through the network until they compromised both the Windows and macOS build environments ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]).

Mandiant reported that the attackers used a compiled version of the open-source **Fast Reverse Proxy** project for lateral movement. A file named `MsMpEng.exe`, with MD5 hash `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`, was dropped in `C:\Windows\System32`. The name imitated a legitimate Microsoft Defender executable, while the file’s reported functionality was associated with the attacker’s internal movement through the 3CX environment ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]).

The attackers then established persistence and execution mechanisms in the build infrastructure:

- On the Windows build environment, they deployed a **TAXHAUL** launcher and **COLDCAT** downloader.
- TAXHAUL persisted through DLL search-order hijacking involving the IKEEXT service and executed with LocalSystem privileges.
- On the macOS build server, they deployed **POOLRAT**, using Launch Daemons for persistence.
- Mandiant clarified that a sample previously described as SIMPLESEA was, after analysis, determined to be POOLRAT ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]).

These findings demonstrate that the attackers did not merely compromise a customer-facing 3CX system. They reached the systems used to build and package 3CX software. That distinction is essential: access to the build environment enabled the attackers to turn a private network intrusion into a software-distribution compromise.

### Stage 3: Compromise of 3CX build outputs

After compromising the build environments, the attackers inserted malicious functionality into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp releases. The affected Windows DesktopApp version identified by Mandiant was **18.12.416 and earlier**. The malicious application included code that executed a downloader called **SUDDENICON**. SUDDENICON extracted command-and-control server information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. It then used the recovered C2 infrastructure to download a further-stage payload called **ICONICSTEALER**, which collected browser information and application configuration data ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]).

The delivery mechanism depended on DLL sideloading. Kaspersky reported that the malicious MSI installer contained an infected DLL that decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll` and executed it. The resulting payload extracted C2 URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository. The initial payload collected system information and browser history, while later stages could deliver more capable malware ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4]).

Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency reported that affected Windows Electron versions included **18.12.407 and 18.12.416**. It also identified affected macOS Electron versions as **18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416**. The agency stated that the trojanized application could harvest system information and steal data and stored credentials from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox profiles ([Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, 2023](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/) [S9]).

Early reporting differed regarding macOS activity. CrowdStrike observed malicious activity on Windows and macOS, while other researchers initially could not confirm the macOS component. Subsequent Mandiant reporting confirmed that the attacker compromised the macOS build environment and used POOLRAT, although this does not mean that every macOS customer installation was malicious or that the same downstream behavior was observed on all platforms ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/) [S1]; [Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]).

### Stage 4: Distribution to 3CX customers

The modified 3CX DesktopApp was distributed through legitimate 3CX channels and was digitally signed by 3CX. CrowdStrike observed suspicious activity from a legitimate signed binary beginning in late March 2023. SentinelOne referred to the operation as “Smooth Operator,” while early reporting described beaconing to attacker-controlled infrastructure, second-stage payload deployment, and, in a small number of cases, hands-on-keyboard activity ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/) [S1]).

The scale of exposure was potentially large. 3CX reportedly had more than 600,000 corporate customers and over 12 million active daily users. Huntress reported more than 242,000 publicly exposed 3CX phone-management systems according to Shodan data, and stated that it had sent 2,595 incident reports involving binaries matching known malicious hashes and signed by 3CX on March 13 ([Cybersecurity Dive, 2023](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/) [S1]). These figures describe potential exposure or observed internet-facing systems, not confirmed compromise. The public evidence does not establish that all 600,000 customers installed a malicious version or that all exposed systems executed the malware.

## Follow-on targeting and Gopuram deployment

The campaign appears to have used the widely distributed first-stage compromise for reconnaissance and victim selection. Kaspersky found that the attackers deployed the more capable **Gopuram** backdoor to fewer than ten machines in the telemetry available to it. Those machines were associated with cryptocurrency companies, leading Kaspersky to characterize the targeting as “surgical precision” ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4]; [WIRED, 2023a](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/) [S2]).

Gopuram was observed through files and persistence mechanisms including:

- `C:\Windows\system32\wlbsctrl.dll`, MD5 `9f85a07d4b4abff82ca18d990f062a84`;
- An encrypted shellcode file under `C:\Windows\System32\config\TxR\`;
- `C:\Windows\system32\catroot2\edb.chk.log`;
- The principal Gopuram module identified as `guard64.dll`.

The malware could interact with the victim’s file system, create processes, and launch in-memory modules. Its modules included capabilities for registry manipulation, service management, timestomping, process injection, network connection, and partial user, group, session, and share management ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4]).

Kaspersky reported no evidence in its observed cases that cryptocurrency had actually been stolen. Therefore, cryptocurrency theft is a well-supported **suspected objective**, not a proven outcome of the 3CX campaign. The targeting hypothesis is strengthened by the use of Gopuram in prior cryptocurrency-related intrusions and its coexistence with AppleJeus, but the supplied evidence does not identify named victim companies or prove successful financial theft ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4]; [WIRED, 2023a](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/) [S2]).

## Public attribution and activity-cluster assessment

### UNC4736 and North Korean nexus

Mandiant tracked the 3CX activity as **UNC4736**, describing it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. The assessment was based on several links:

1. Similarities between the compromised X_TRADER and 3CX applications.
2. Shared use of the SIGFLIP and DAVESHELL loading methodology.
3. Shared use of the RC4 key `3jB(2bsG#@c7`.
4. Shared use of the cookie variable `__tutma`.
5. Similarities in AES-256-GCM communications.
6. POOLRAT overlap with an older sample associated with the trojanized CoinGoTrade application.
7. Infrastructure relationships involving domains such as `journalide[.]org`.
8. Historical Google TAG reporting concerning the compromise of `www.tradingtechnologies[.]com` and North Korean AppleJeus activity ([Mandiant, 2023](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise) [S3]; [Google TAG, 2022](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/) [S5]).

Google TAG had previously reported that a North Korean group associated with Operation AppleJeus targeted cryptocurrency and fintech organizations. TAG observed the compromise of `www.tradingtechnologies[.]com` in February 2022, before the distribution of compromised X_TRADER updates described by Mandiant. TAG also connected the broader activity to exploitation of Chrome vulnerability CVE-2022-0609 and targeting of cryptocurrency and fintech users ([Google TAG, 2022](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/) [S5]).

### Lazarus, Labyrinth Chollima, and naming uncertainty

Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram deployment to Lazarus with medium to high confidence. Its reasoning included Gopuram’s previous coexistence with AppleJeus on a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency company’s network, infrastructure overlap with domains previously attributed to Lazarus, and similarities in loader shellcode and the `DllGetClassObject` API-hash pattern ([Kaspersky, 2023](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/) [S4]).

MITRE ATT&CK identifies AppleJeus as malware used by Lazarus Group and describes AppleJeus as a downloader family initially found in trojanized cryptocurrency applications. MITRE also associates Lazarus Group with multiple aliases, including Labyrinth Chollima, HIDDEN COBRA, ZINC, NICKEL ACADEMY, and Diamond Sleet. However, MITRE cautions that North Korean cyber units share personnel, infrastructure, malware, and tradecraft, making precise subgroup attribution difficult ([MITRE, 2025](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/) [S6]; [MITRE, 2026](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/) [S7]).

Early reporting from CrowdStrike named Labyrinth Chollima, while a WIRED article described the relevant actor using names including Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, or Velvet Chollima. Those labels should not be treated as interchangeable proof of a single organizational identity. The reporting reflects different vendor naming conventions and varying attribution judgments. Mandiant’s more precise operational designation, UNC4736, is therefore preferable for the 3CX-specific activity, with Lazarus/AppleJeus representing the broader publicly reported association.

## Contradictions and unresolved questions

| Issue | Evidence tension | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Exact threat-actor name | CrowdStrike reporting used Labyrinth Chollima; WIRED used Kimsuky/Emerald Sleet/Velvet Chollima; Mandiant used UNC4736; Kaspersky used Lazarus. | These should be treated as attribution labels with different confidence and scope, not as definitive proof that all names identify one identical subgroup. |
| macOS compromise | Early reporting said macOS activity was not independently confirmed by all researchers. | Mandiant later confirmed compromise of the macOS build environment and identified POOLRAT, but customer-level macOS impact remains less clearly documented. |
| Victim count | 600,000 customers and 242,000 exposed systems describe potential reach, while fewer than ten Gopuram victims were observed by Kaspersky. | Broad initial exposure and narrow follow-on targeting are compatible; the figures measure different stages of the campaign. |
| Cryptocurrency theft | Reporting strongly suggests cryptocurrency-related targeting, but Kaspersky observed no confirmed theft. | Cryptocurrency theft is a suspected objective, not a proven result in the supplied evidence. |
| Initial X_TRADER compromise | Mandiant identified the compromised installer as the entry point but did not investigate how Trading Technologies’ software was altered. | The first known step in the public chain is established, but the deeper origin of that compromise is unknown. |

## Conclusion

The public evidence supports a concrete cascading supply-chain model:

**Compromised Trading Technologies X_TRADER installer → 3CX employee endpoint → lateral movement and credential harvesting inside 3CX → compromise of Windows and macOS build environments → trojanized, legitimately signed 3CX DesktopApp releases → broad customer exposure → selective deployment of ICONICSTEALER and, in fewer than ten observed cases, Gopuram.**

The initiating event was therefore not simply “hackers infected 3CX customers.” It was a prior software supply-chain compromise that gave the attackers access to 3CX, followed by compromise of 3CX’s software-production infrastructure. Mandiant’s UNC4736 designation is the most suitable case-specific activity-cluster identifier in the supplied evidence. The wider public attribution is to a North Korea-linked, financially motivated ecosystem associated with AppleJeus and Lazarus, but the exact subgroup identity remains uncertain. The evidence supports high confidence in the cascading supply-chain mechanism and moderate confidence in the specific UNC4736-to-AppleJeus relationship; it does not support a definitive claim regarding successful cryptocurrency theft or the complete universe of victims.
